power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p-values > .001", Text = "Overall, most demographic variables measured at baseline were not significantly (all p-values > .001) predictive of attrition status."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p-values > .001", "p = .694"), Sentence = c("Overall, most demographic variables measured at baseline were not significantly (all p-values > .001) predictive of attrition status.", "The EXT PGS was negatively associated with the RI from the youth-report of positive parenting (β = -.06) but not parent report (β = -.01, p = .694)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. text.text: Background: Parenting practices are a potential mechanism through which adolescent delinquent behavior can be modified.
However, it remains unclear whether associations between parenting and delinquency reflect stable differences between families or dynamic processes unfolding within families over time.

The current study disentangled the between-and within-person associations between delinquency and parenting across adolescence and whether genetic propensity toward externalizing, indexed by a polygenic score (EXT PGS), was associated with stable between-person differences in delinquency and parenting Methods: Participants were 2,184 adolescents assessed annually from ages 12 to 17 as part of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development-Social Development sub-study.
Parents and youth reported on delinquency and parenting dimensions (corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, poor monitoring, positive parenting).
Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models separated between-person and within-person associations.
We evaluated the association between the EXT PGS and the random intercepts.

Results: Between-persons, adolescents with higher average delinquency experienced higher average levels of corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring and lower positive parenting.

EXT PGS was associated with higher levels of delinquency and with higher corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, as well as lower youthreported positive parenting and accounted for approximately 4%-8% of variance shared between delinquency and parenting.
Within-person, higher delinquency was associated with subsequent increases in youth-reported corporal punishment, but not parent-reported corporal punishment.
Reciprocal associations emerged between delinquency and poor monitoring in both parent-and youth-report models and between delinquency and youth-reported inconsistent discipline.
No longitudinal associations emerged between positive parenting and delinquency.
Conclusions: Associations between parenting and delinquency reflected both stable individual differences and dynamic developmental processes.
The EXT PGS contributed to stable differences in delinquency and parenting, while longitudinal associations varied across parenting dimensions.
These findings suggest that a focus on decreasing inconsistent discipline and increasing parental monitoring may be particularly relevant for mitigating delinquency.

Delinquent behaviors (e.g., rule breaking, aggression, and other antisocial behaviors), fall within the broader domain of externalizing behavior 1 and represent a costly public health problem, with links to substance use disorders, legal system involvement, and broader psychosocial dysfunction. 2, 3 Mean-levels of delinquency follow an age-related pattern 3, 4 , with behaviors increasing during adolescence, as youth have increased independence and autonomy over their activities, behaviors, and peer groups.

text.text: The parent-child relationship has been identified as a particularly important factor that can modify risk for engaging in delinquent behaviors.

Harsh and inconsistent disciplinary practices, poor parental monitoring, and low levels of positive involvement are all associated with increased risk for delinquent behavior among adolescents. 5, 6 However, we must understand how parenting practices and delinquent behavior co-develop, parsing between-and within-person effects, to inform etiology as well as identify targets for early intervention.

text.text: Theories regarding the development of delinquent behavior posit that negative child-parent transactions may increase the risk of increased delinquent behavior over the course of development. 7, 8 Parenting practices, such as discipline, monitoring, and involvement, as well as adolescent delinquency may directly influence each other through within-person, reciprocal processes.
text.formatted: Theories regarding the development of delinquent behavior posit that negative child-parent transactions may increase the risk of increased delinquent behavior over the course of development. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> Parenting practices, such as discipline, monitoring, and involvement, as well as adolescent delinquency may directly influence each other through within-person, reciprocal processes.

text.text: For example, a child engaging in increased delinquent behavior may lead to a change in their parents' behaviors.
If their parents' reaction is to increase supervision and monitoring, this may lead to a subsequent decrease in delinquent behavior.
However, if increased delinquent behavior leads to parents' implementing increasingly harsh punishments, these actions may serve to exacerbate delinquent behavior.

Therefore, if we can understand how these processes develop over time, intervention can be applied to disrupt these reciprocal relationships and deflect trajectories of adolescent delinquent behavior.

Despite the importance of understanding how this developmental process unfolds, research to formally tease apart these developmental trajectories has been hampered by small sample sizes and methodological approaches that conflate between-and within-person processes, which has produced overall inconsistent results.

For example, some studies have found that positive parenting in childhood is protective against risk taking during adolescence 9 , while others have found that youth behavior impacts parental monitoring, but not the reciprocal effect 10 , while other studies have found evidence for a bidirectional longitudinal association between delinquency and parenting practices. 11 For these studies, sample sizes were relatively small (N's <500) and many used cross-lagged panel models (CLPM) which cannot parse the between-and within-person associations between variables needed to isolate short-term, dynamic effects. 5, 6 One method for addressing this is the random intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM), which extends the traditional CLPM by accounting for the between-person developmental trends in variables of interest (e.g., between-person trajectory of delinquency over time) along with the fluctuating within-person auto-regressive (e.g., within-person effect of delinquency over time) and cross-lagged (e.g., the within-person association of delinquency at time one on parental involvement at time two).

text.text: One recent study employing RI-CLPMs to disentangle the development of externalizing behaviors and parenting has found evidence for reciprocal associations between parental monitoring and aggression 12 ; however, another study examining the association between parental knowledge and externalizing behavior found no evidence for within-person cross-lagged associations from ages 8-15. 13 Therefore, additional research is needed to more fully characterize the association between delinquency and parenting, including behaviors beyond just parental knowledge and monitoring.

text.text: Both delinquency and parenting behaviors are individually heritable, and the association between parenting and adolescent externalizing behaviors is itself partly genetically influenced. 14, 15 Genetically informed designs suggest that these influences can operate through multiple pathways.

text.text: They can work passively, when parents transmit both genes and rearing environment, or evocatively, when youths' heritable characteristics elicit parenting responses.

Evidence has generally favored evocative processes. [16] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] Regardless of pathway, these findings suggest that part of the association between parenting and delinquency may reflect shared genetic propensity rather than purely environmental transmission.

text.text: Such effects would be expected to show up largely as stable differences between families, the component that RI-CLPMs separate from within-person dynamics.
Measured genetic data, such as polygenic scores (PGS), offer a complementary approach.

One study found that youths' genetic propensity toward externalizing behavior was associated with both higher youth externalizing behavior and lower parental monitoring and knowledge. 22 Because youth PGS capture variants inherited from parents, associations between youth PGS and parenting may reflect passive or evocative processes, which cannot be distinguished without parental genotypes.

text.text: However, youth PGS can index the extent to which stable betweenperson differences in delinquency and parenting, and the overlap between them, are associated with genetic propensity toward externalizing.
Integrating a PGS into the RI-CLPM framework therefore makes it possible to quantify how much of the stable association between delinquency and parenting is linked to genetic propensity.

The current study disentangled the between and within-person associations between delinquency and parenting practices during adolescence using RI-CLPMs using data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development-Social Development (ABCD-SD) Study.
This sub study of the ABCD study focuses on measuring self-and caregiver-report data on delinquency and victimization as well as including detailed assessment of parenting practices.

We also examined the role of genetic propensity towards externalizing, measured via a polygenic score (EXT PGS), on the development of both delinquency and parenting behaviors, to quantify the role of genetics on this process.
We hypothesized that over time, levels of delinquency would increase, consistent with results from other epidemiologic samples examining delinquency during this developmental period.

We also anticipated that facets of parenting including supervision and monitoring, would decrease over time, consistent with previous studies showing that parental oversight declines as youth gain autonomy. 23 We further predicted that the EXT PGS would be associated with the between-person, mean levels of delinquency and parenting practices over time.

text.text: Regarding within-person effects, we hypothesized that there would be significant cross-lagged associations between delinquency scores and parenting behavior scores.
However, given that previous studies have been limited in power and found mixed results, we did not advance specific hypotheses regarding the direction of effects.
Data were drawn from waves 1-6 of the ABCD-SD study (Release 7.0).

text.text: Delinquency was measured with the Self-Reported Delinquency Scale (SRD) 24 .

text.text: In this 48-item measure, informants reported on a variety of delinquent behaviors including vandalism, theft, violence, and harassment.
At the baseline ABCD-SD visit participants were asked about these behaviors occurring during their lifetime as well as in the past 12 months.
At subsequent study visits participants report on the event happening "since the previous SD study visit".
The current analyses only used the past 12 months measure from baseline to ensure measurement was consistent across time.

Nine items were excluded due to being outcomes of delinquent behavior (e.g., arrest, suspension) or not an indicator of delinquency (e.g., fighting with a sibling; items listed in Supplemental Methods).
Informants (parent and child) also indicated if the behavior has been done "never" (coded as 0), "once or twice" (coded as 1) or "more often" (coded as 2).

As parents and youth often have access to different information about delinquent behavior, integrating reports across informants allows behaviors reported by either source to contribute to the overall score.

Consistent with this multi-informant approach and because our analyses focused on overall levels of delinquency rather than informant-specific perspectives, we chose to summed responses across reporters.
This resulted in a Delinquency score with a possible range from 0-156, reflecting delinquent behaviors a youth has engaged in during the past 12 months at each wave of data collection.

Parenting behaviors were measured by the Alabama Parenting Questionnaire (APQ). 25 APQ assesses five constructs: Use of corporal punishment, Inconsistent discipline, Poor supervision and monitoring, Positive involvement with children, and Use of positive parenting techniques.

text.text: For the purposes of these analyses, and consistent with previous studies of the factor structure of the APQ, 26 we combined the Positive involvement and Use of positive parenting techniques scales into one scale by summing across all items (Positive parenting).

text.text: These subscales are highly correlated and often load onto a single factor in adolescent samples.
Both child and parent completed the APQ and we anticipated that reporters would differ on their assessment of parenting behaviors.
We therefore examined four APQ subscales separately for each reporter (eight reporter-specific measures in total).

Two-tailed p-values and 95% confidence intervals were computed based on the pooled estimates and standard errors.

We modeled the co-development of delinquency and parenting behaviors in 8 separate RI-CLPMs, modeling delinquency with each parenting subscale for each reporter (delinquency with 4 subscales, per reporter).
Family ID was included as random effects in all models.
These models fit two random intercepts to account for stable between-person differences in delinquency and parenting across time.

Within-person fluctuations were modeled using autoregressive paths (AR) within each construct and cross-lagged (CL) paths between delinquency and parenting across time, along with within-wave covariances between the withinperson components.

AR paths capture the persistence of within-person deviations within each construct across time, and the CL paths test whether a deviation from a child's expected level of delinquency is associated with a subsequent deviation from their expected level of parenting behavior at the next wave, controlling for the prior within-person level of parenting behavior, and vice versa.

To identify the most parsimonious model, we compared parameters between a fully constrained (all CL paths of the same direction and AR paths for each variable constrained to the same value over time) and fully unconstrained (all CL and AR paths allowed to vary over time) models.
Changes in model fit were evaluated using chi-square difference test.
As outlined by 41 , we included the EXT PGS as a time-invariant predictor on each best fitting RI-CLPM.

For each best-fitting RI-CLPM there were significant associations between the random intercepts.

Random intercept (RI) factors for delinquency were positively associated with the RI factors for corporal punishment (parent-report r = .32; youth-report r =.28), inconsistent discipline (parent-report r =.35; youth-report r = .34), and poor monitoring (parent-report r =.33; youth-report r = .35), and negatively associated with the RI for positive parenting (parent-report r = -.21; youth-report r = -.25).

These results indicated that youth who exhibited higher levels of delinquency on average across ages 12-17 also experienced higher levels of corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, and lower levels of positive parenting.

The EXT PGS was significantly associated with delinquency RIs across all models (βs ~ .17) as well as significantly associated with RIs for corporal punishment (parent-report β = .11; youth-report β =.13), inconsistent discipline (parent-report β = .10; youthreport β =.12), and poor monitoring (parent-report β = .07; youth-report β =.11).
The EXT PGS was negatively associated with the RI from the youth-report of positive parenting (β = -.06) but not parent report (β = -.01, p = .694).

Based on these results, the EXT PGS accounted for about 6-8% of the between-person association between delinquency and corporal punishment, 5-6% of the between-person association between delinquency and inconsistent discipline, 4-5% of the between-person association between delinquency and poor monitoring, and 4% of the betweenperson association between delinquency and youth-report of positive parenting.

text.text: The present study examined the longitudinal interplay between delinquency and multiple dimensions of parenting during adolescence, while explicitly distinguishing stable betweenperson differences from within-person developmental processes.

Consistent with prior metaanalytic evidence, we found robust between-person associations between delinquency and multiple dimensions of parenting. 5, 6 However, the within-person findings revealed a more nuanced picture: adolescent delinquency consistently predicted subsequent increases in corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, while poor monitoring and youth-report of inconsistent discipline were predictive of subsequent delinquency as well.
text.formatted: Consistent with prior metaanalytic evidence, we found robust between-person associations between delinquency and multiple dimensions of parenting. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> However, the within-person findings revealed a more nuanced picture: adolescent delinquency consistently predicted subsequent increases in corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, while poor monitoring and youth-report of inconsistent discipline were predictive of subsequent delinquency as well.

text.text: In contrast, positive parenting, which is comprised of items related to positive involvement and use of positive parenting techniques, was associated with lower delinquency at the between-person level but showed no prospective within-person associations with delinquency.
Finally, the EXT PGS was associated with stable levels of both delinquency and several parenting dimensions.

Together, these findings provide evidence for a transactional interplay between certain parenting behaviors and adolescent delinquency in which stable individual and family characteristics coexist with dynamic processes through which adolescents and parents shape one another over time.

At the between-person level, youth who exhibited higher average levels of delinquency across ages 12-17 also experienced higher average levels of corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring and lower average levels of positive parenting, with associations similar across parent-and youth-report models.

This pattern is consistent with a large literature demonstrating that parenting behaviors, particularly parental monitoring and harsh and neglectful parenting, are associated with adolescent delinquency. 5, 6 The EXT PGS was associated with the random intercepts for both delinquency and parenting, indicating that genetic propensity towards externalizing is linked to these stable between-person differences.

text.text: Because youth PGS reflect variants inherited from parents, these associations may arise through passive processes (parents transmitting both genetic risk and a rearing environment), evocative processes (youths' genetically influenced characteristics eliciting particular parenting responses), or both.
Distinguishing these pathways will require designs that include parental genotypes, such as trio or within-family PGS approaches.

Because the RI-CLPM partitions stable between-person variance from within-person change, the within-person associations discussed below are independent of these stable, partly genetically influenced differences.

The within-person cross-lagged results provide evidence of prospective associations between adolescent delinquency and subsequent parenting behaviors, particularly poor monitoring and youth-reported inconsistent discipline, where we found evidence for reciprocal within-person associations.

Across both parent-and youth-report models, higher-than-expected levels of poor monitoring was associated with subsequent increases in delinquency, while higher-than-expected delinquency also was associated with subsequent increases in poor monitoring.
Thus, poor monitoring and delinquency appear to be embedded in a reciprocal feedback process, whereby changes in one construct are followed by changes in the other.
Several mechanisms may account for this cycle.

On one side, parents facing escalating delinquent behavior may become worn down or discouraged, and may withdraw from monitoring efforts they perceive as ineffective or not worth the conflict they provoke. 43, 44 Youth engaging in delinquency may also become more secretive and disclose less about their activities, further limiting parents' knowledge of their whereabouts and companions. 45 On the other side, reduced supervision gives youth more unstructured, unsupervised time and greater opportunity to affiliate with deviant peers, a robust proximal predictor of delinquent behavior. 46 Over time, these processes may amplify one another, with each increase in delinquency further eroding monitoring and each lapse in monitoring creating new opportunities for delinquent behavior.

text.text: We found similar evidence for youth-reported inconsistent discipline, suggesting that adolescents' behavior may be associated with subsequent changes in how parents monitor and discipline them.

Although parental monitoring has traditionally been conceptualized primarily as a parental influence on adolescent behavior, developmental research increasingly demonstrates that adolescents' behavior can also shape parents' monitoring practices. 47 Our findings also align with prior evidence identifying parental monitoring as one of the parenting dimensions most strongly associated with adolescent delinquency. 5, 6 Moreover, prior longitudinal research has documented reciprocal associations between parental behavioral control, which included monitoring and discipline, and delinquency, 48, 49 with some evidence suggesting that these associations may be stronger during adolescence than childhood. 6 Together, these findings highlight the importance of conceptualizing parenting and adolescent delinquency as dynamically interrelated processes rather than as unidirectional influences.

text.text: There was also a unidirectional within-person association from delinquency to youthreport of corporal punishment, such that higher-than-expected levels of delinquency predicted higher-than-expected levels of corporal punishment at subsequent assessments.

These associations remained after accounting for stable between-person differences and prior withinperson deviations in both constructs, suggesting that increases in adolescent delinquency may prompt increases in punitive parental responses.

Much of the parenting and delinquency literature has focused on identifying parenting behaviors that predict subsequent delinquency; however, these results highlight that adolescent behavior itself may be an important contributor to changes in parenting behaviors during early and middle adolescence.

Given the known negative outcomes associated with use of corporal punishment, 50, 51 these results suggest the potential value of providing resources and support to parents whose children are exhibiting problem behaviors to promote more effective, non-punitive parenting behaviors.

text.text: The findings for positive parenting provide an important counterpoint to the results from corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline and poor monitoring.

At the between-person level, youth who experienced consistently higher levels of positive parenting across adolescence also exhibited lower levels of delinquency, consistent with the broader literature linking supportive and responsive parenting with more adaptive adolescent outcomes. 5, 6 Yet, at the within-person level, higher-than-usual positive parenting was not associated with subsequent deviations in delinquency, nor was higher-than-usual delinquency associated with subsequent changes in positive parenting.

text.text: This divergence between between-person and within-person effects suggests that the protective association of positive parenting may reflect stable characteristics of youth and families rather than short-term fluctuations in positive parenting.

Families characterized by consistently high levels of positive parenting may also differ in other stable characteristics (e.g., family functioning, socioeconomic resources, broader environmental supports) that contribute to lower levels of delinquency.

Therefore, while positive parenting is still important to the development of delinquency, these results suggest that the association between positive parenting and delinquency may operate differently from the dynamic processes observed for adverse parenting.
Several limitations should be considered.
First, although the RI-CLPM provides an improvement over traditional cross-lagged models, the cross-lagged effects should not be interpreted as causal effects.

The models cannot rule out unmeasured time-varying factors that influence both parenting and delinquency, and temporal precedence alone is insufficient to establish causality. 41, 52 Second, the EXT PGS was based on EUR-only GWAS summary statistics.

text.text: EUR-only GWAS have decreased power and accuracy in non-EUR samples and has the potential to bias estimates from the pooled PGS analyses reported here.
Therefore, these results will need to be replicated as multiancestry GWAS summary statistics become available.
In addition, ABCD sample is now in mid-adolescence (Mage = 16.58, SD = 0.94 at the most recent assessment), and data from the later waves of data collection remain incomplete.
Thus, these analyses will need to be extended as additional waves become available, and the sample progresses through adolescence.

Taken together, these findings support a developmental model in which adolescent delinquency emerges from the intersection of stable individual differences, genetic propensity, and dynamic family processes.
The results are broadly consistent with transactional models of development and demonstrate that reciprocity is not uniform across parenting behaviors.
Rather, the direction and strength of prospective associations depend on the specific parenting behavior being considered.

The reciprocal association between poor monitoring and delinquency suggests that interventions may benefit from simultaneously addressing adolescent behavior and parental monitoring rather than treating either as an isolated target, consistent with intervention models that conceptualize adolescent externalizing problems within the broader family system.

Moreover, because delinquency was associated with subsequent increases in corporal punishment, inconsistent discipline, and poor monitoring, interventions to help parents disrupt this feedback loop (e.g., the Family Check Up 53 ) may be particularly valuable for supporting effective parental responses to escalating adolescent behavior.

What's known?

• Parenting practices and adolescent delinquency are consistently associated, but these links may reflect both stable individual differences and dynamic developmental processes that previous studies have been unable to disentangle.
• This study disentangled stable between-person associations from longitudinal withinperson processes across adolescence.
• Genetic propensity for externalizing was associated with stable differences in both delinquency and parenting, accounting for approximately 4%-8% of shared variance.

• Within-person associations varied by parenting dimension: delinquency was associated with increases in youth-reported corporal punishment, while delinquency and poor monitoring showed reciprocal associations.
What's relevant?

• Clinical interventions targeting adolescent delinquency may benefit from simultaneously addressing parenting behaviors and providing supports and resources specifically for parents to strengthen parental monitoring and promote consistent, non-punitive responses to adolescent behavior.
